title: Oil Prices Jump to $105 as Middle East Conflict Grows
summary:
Have you ever seen the price of something go up really fast? That's happening right now with oil — the stuff that becomes gasoline for cars, trucks, and airplanes.

On Wednesday, the price of Brent crude oil went back above $100 a barrel and kept climbing to $105. Why? Because fighting between the US and Iran in the Middle East is getting worse, and it doesn't look like it will end soon.

The conflict has closed the Strait of Hormuz — a narrow waterway that ships oil and gas from the Gulf to the rest of the world. Think of it like a giant highway for oil tankers. If the highway is blocked, the oil can't get through, and prices go up.

Natural gas prices are rising too. In the UK, gas went above 200p a therm for the first time since the end of 2022. Europe's storage levels are lower than normal, and countries need to fill them before winter.

There's more. Long-term borrowing costs for the US and UK are at their highest in decades. That means governments pay more to borrow money — and it can affect things like mortgage rates for families.

President Trump spoke at a Republican convention in Texas on Wednesday. He said he doesn't think the fighting will end until after the US midterm elections in November. Also, Iran-aligned Houthi forces reportedly seized Yemen's port of Mokha, a key Red Sea port, which could cause even more shipping problems.
why_it_matters: Oil prices reach into your life through the school bus, the family car and the price of food, so fighting far away can still change what things cost at home.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz (a narrow stretch of water between the Gulf and the open ocean) is one of the world's most important oil routes, and a huge share of the oil countries buy travels through it.
Brent crude oil is named after an oil field in the North Sea (the sea between the UK and Norway), but its price is used worldwide as a sign of how much oil costs.
Oil prices have jumped suddenly before, like during Middle East conflicts in the 1970s, when long lines formed at gas stations in the United States.
Article_Structure: WHO: Oil traders and shipping companies, the US and Iran, and Iran-aligned Houthi forces in Yemen.
WHAT: Oil prices climbed past $100 a barrel and reached $105 because fighting in the Middle East closed the Strait of Hormuz.
WHERE: The Middle East — especially the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf, and Yemen's port of Mokha on the Red Sea — with effects felt in the US, UK and Europe.
WHY: When oil and gas cannot move through the waterway, fuel gets more expensive, which pushes up heating and borrowing costs for families.

perspectives.description: They earn more when prices rise, so higher prices can mean bigger profits for the companies that produce and ship fuel.
They pay more at the gas pump and for heating, and higher borrowing costs can make house payments harder to afford.
They warn that a closed Strait of Hormuz and trouble near the Red Sea could push prices even higher if the fighting lasts into winter.
